rationale: A class nested in a class body is a MEMBER of it: `Outer.Inner` resolves in Python with no lookup machinery, so the nesting is containment. This is the first genuine ANALYZER defect the independent oracle found — 66 `contains` edges across 24 corpus files that the tree supports and the lane did not emit, including `_Multipart._Part` in urllib/parse.py. Nothing else had seen it, because `contains` is derived from `ownerName` and a nested class had none. The two positive rows are the fix; the forbid row is the half that is easy to get wrong in the eager direction, since a class written inside a METHOD is a LOCAL of that method — `Outer.Deep` does not resolve, so publishing that edge would add a name to the outer class's surface that the source does not give it. A fix that only added the containment would pass both positive rows and fail this one, which is the point of writing it. The `ownerName` row is load-bearing outside this lane: the indexer keys `nameToSymbol` on `${scope || ownerName}.${name}` as well as `name`, so a nested class with an owner resolves its own `overrides` sources exactly rather than falling back to a first-wins leaf lookup — the dependency `python/owner-name-stripped` exercises, and the one the retracted PY-3 turned out to rest on.

expectSymbols.name: Inner
expectSymbols.note: the member a nested class now is. Before the fix this symbol existed with NO owner, so no `contains` was derived for it and the class was unreachable from its parent

expectSymbols.name: Local
expectSymbols.note: a class in a METHOD: still a symbol, and still ownerless. `Outer.Local` does not resolve in Python, so it must not acquire an owner

expectSymbols.name: AlsoLocal
expectSymbols.note: a class in a plain function: same rule, one scope down

expectSymbols.name: Sibling
expectSymbols.note: a module-level class is ownerless — Python has no module declaration, which is the scripting-family contract

expectRelationships.note: THE FIX. A class written in a class body is a member of that class
the nested class's own members belong to the nested class, not one level up

forbidRelationships.note: THE BOUNDARY. `Local` is declared inside `outer_method`, so it is a local of that method and `Outer.Local` does not resolve. The fix keys on `currentClass && !currentFunction` precisely so this edge is not published; a fix that only added containment would pass every positive row and fail here

_seamNote.what: Class nesting is containment one level down and locality everywhere else. A `class` written in a class body gets `ownerName`; a `class` written in a method body or a function body does not.
_seamNote.why: The reachable/not-reachable line is Python's own, not a convention chosen here: `Outer.Inner` resolves through the class body's namespace, and a name bound in a method's body is gone when the method returns. Publishing the second as a member of the first would make the outer class's surface larger than the language's, and a graph that overstates a surface is worse than one that understates it — an overstatement sends a reader to a name that cannot be resolved, while an understatement is visible as a gap. Entering a class clears `currentFunction` and entering a function sets it, so the two cases are distinguishable during the single walk with no extra state, and the guard is one clause rather than a stack.
